label: inadequate hood coverage
description:
A directly visible grease/smoke-producing appliance with visibly inadequate hood coverage, subject to the evidence requirements below. Eligible appliances include fryers, griddles, charbroilers, open ranges, woks, salamanders/broilers, and conveyor pizza ovens. Never infer an appliance from a suppression system, tank, pipe, or service tag.
Wall- or table-mounted broilers/salamanders qualify as grease-producing appliances requiring a hood; do not dismiss them as conveyor toasters. Countertop/low-grease units such as conveyor toasters, microwaves, food warmers, steam kettles, and dishwashers do not qualify.
Check every grease-producing appliance, including portable units on side tables, items at the far left/right of the line, and anything in a gap between two hoods.
A hood is an overhead canopy with a grease-filter bank. The following are NOT hoods and do not provide coverage: a wire rack, an open wall shelf, a salamander/storage shelf, or any shelving above an appliance. A grease appliance sitting under only a shelf or rack lacks coverage.
Apply this label only with positive proof of at least one of the following:
- The ceiling directly above the appliance is visible, and the full gap between the appliance and ceiling is clearly free of any hood. Seeing the ceiling or a wall above an appliance is NOT by itself proof of a missing hood, because a hood frequently mounts to the side or extends out of frame. Only conclude "no hood" when the appliance's entire overhead envelope—including every side where a hood could attach—is visible in-frame and unobstructed.
- The hood's physical front or side edge—not the photo border—is visible, and the appliance clearly continues past it. Do not treat a hood's end skirt, triangular end, or side canopy panel as the terminal filter edge. To judge whether an appliance is past the canopy, check what it backs onto: an appliance set against a plain wall, backsplash, or a vertical pipe—rather than the hood's own backsplash—is outside the footprint.
Do not apply this label if the hood, the space above the appliance, or the ceiling is cut off, out of frame, blurred, or otherwise unconfirmable. A tight crop alone does not establish inadequate coverage. Do not apply this label when steep angles or perspective distortion make it ambiguous whether the appliance extends past the hood's edge.
Appliances with their own integral/attached hood, filter unit, or ventless recirculating ventilation are adequately covered—do not apply this label to them.
When the proof requirements are met, apply this label if the appliance is outside the Type I hood footprint, under a Type II/non-grease vent, or lacks approximately 6 inches of overhang. Type I hoods have vertical slatted metal grease baffles; Type II hoods show wire mesh, honeycomb, or flat plates (and often no fire-suppression nozzle) and serve heat/steam applications rather than grease-producing appliances. A Type II vent directly over a grease-producing appliance (e.g., a fryer or range) is inadequate coverage—apply the label.
In the classification explanation, cite the ceiling, hood-edge, shelf/rack, or Type II filter evidence.

label: hood missing filter
description:
A commercial kitchen exhaust hood with a whole filter panel absent, leaving an opening through the filter plane within the rack.
First locate the filter rack using installed panel borders and retaining rails. Inspect every visible section, including both ends and image boundaries. A panel missing at the far left/right end of the bank, or a bank that is entirely empty with all filters absent, both qualify—do not require the whole rack to be brightly lit; a clearly exposed empty rack is sufficient even in shadow.
Confirm the missing panel using both:
- Exposed rack edges, supports, or recessed space behind the opening; and
- An opening consistent with a complete filter panel, based on nearby panel boundaries and local perspective.
A panel contains multiple baffle channels. Narrow slits between installed panels or along their edges are bypass gaps, not missing filters—even when they extend the full filter height. A single filter that is slanted, dislodged, off its track, or has a damaged channel is a bypass gap, not a missing filter.
Perspective alone does not establish a missing panel. Exclude: the inner end of the hood canopy or plenum space (which is not a filter slot), ordinary canopy space around lights or piping, solid blanking panels, hood end/side walls, and self-cleaning/water-wash filters whose design includes a top opening with no baffle channels. Do not identify a filter rack where none is present. Darkness or visible hood interior alone is insufficient unless an empty rack is clearly exposed.
Partial cropping or a crossing pipe does not negate an otherwise identifiable missing panel. If no filters remain, require a visibly exposed empty filter rack. Do not apply this label when no panel-sized absence is established.
In the classification explanation, identify the opening's location and supporting rack evidence.

label: hood grease buildup
description:
Visible grease deposit on an interior surface of a commercial kitchen exhaust hood: panels, filters, visible baffle-channel interiors, or filter rails/troughs.
First confirm that the affected surface belongs to the hood interior. Exterior canopy faces, nearby walls, backsplashes, and cooking equipment do not qualify. Inspect each visible area, especially channel recesses, lower filter edges, seams, and the rails above and below the filters.
Thick or caked buildup is NOT required. Apply this label when any eligible interior area shows a deposited grease feature, including:
- A tacky, filmy, or textured grease coating forming irregular patches, streaks, or layering across a filter face, channel, or multiple baffles.
- Yellow, orange, or brown grease discoloration or staining of the interior metal (as distinct from plain gray metal aging).
- Grease dripping, hanging in droplets, leaving residue-bearing drip trails, or pooling—including drips along or below the filter rails/track.
- Raised, crusted, lumpy, burnt-looking, or caked grease.
A clean-looking surrounding surface does not negate a qualifying deposit. Deposits may be thin as long as they are clearly grease rather than a reflection.
Exclude: a thin, uniform light grease film consistent with normal operational use; scattered fine specks without a coating; reflections, shadows, soot alone, corrosion, water/condensation, cleaning marks, adhesive/sticker residue, and pipe fittings/sealant; a grease collection cup or trough catching grease as designed; and minor metal discoloration from age rather than grease.
Do not apply this label if no qualifying deposit is visible or its interior location cannot be established. Do not infer hidden buildup.
In the classification explanation, identify the affected component, its location, and the specific deposit feature (color, texture, drip) supporting the label.

label: fryer missing baffle
description:
A deep-fat fryer beside an open-flame appliance without an adequate separating baffle, with all of the following clearly visible:
1. A deep-fat fryer with a visible oil vat and fry basket(s) beside an open-flame appliance. The open-flame appliance is identified by exposed flame or open burner grates; an open-burner range and a wok burner both qualify as flame sources. A flat-top griddle, enclosed oven, salamander, and other fryers do NOT qualify as the flame source. A fry basket resting on a table, counter, or inside a wok is NOT a fryer; identify the fryer by its own oil vat, not by a loose basket.
2. Both the edge of the fryer and the edge of the adjacent flame appliance, and the full gap between them, must be clearly visible. If either appliance's edge is out of frame or occluded, do not apply this label—you cannot confirm the absence of a baffle you cannot see.
3. The appliances are directly adjacent, approximately 16 inches or less apart, with no appliance, table, or object between them. If any appliance or object (e.g., a side table, a griddle, a bucket) sits between the fryer and the flame source, they are not directly adjacent.
4. The intervening gap has no solid steel or tempered-glass baffle approximately 8 inches or taller, or the baffle is clearly too short or misplaced to separate the fryer from the open-flame appliance.
Inspect the gap between the appliances directly. A baffle may be thin and hard to see from a head-on angle—do not conclude "no baffle" unless the gap is clearly visible and you can positively confirm the absence of any divider. Rear walls and backsplashes do not count as separating baffles. Do not assume fryer width equals 16 inches; estimate the separation from visible cues and state your basis. In side or oblique views, perspective distorts apparent distance—if the viewing angle makes the separation or the presence of a baffle unreliable to judge, do not apply this label.
Do not apply this label if a qualifying baffle is present, separation exceeds approximately 16 inches, the flame source is actually a griddle or other non-flame appliance, a loose basket (not a fryer vat) is the only "fryer" present, or the appliance edges/gap are out of frame, occluded, or at an angle too steep to confirm any required condition.

label: hood bypass gap
description:
A filter bypass gap in a commercial kitchen exhaust hood: any visible opening at a filter's edge, seam, or channel that lets air bypass the filter media because the filter is improperly seated, aligned, oriented, or sized, or the filter or frame is damaged. Such gaps are common and often subtle—inspect carefully and do not default to "properly seated."
Inspect every visible filter across the bank, including both ends. The following all qualify as bypass gaps:
- An opening between two adjacent filter panels, including a gap at or beside the handles where the panels meet.
- An opening between an end filter and the hood's side frame, side wall, or end of the rack.
- An opening along a filter's top or bottom edge where it meets the frame rail, exposing space behind the filter plane.
- A tilted, bowed, recessed, protruding, dislodged, or off-track filter that creates an opening or wedge at a corner, edge, or seam.
- A bent, cracked, or damaged filter or baffle channel leaving an unobstructed opening behind the filter plane.
- An incorrectly oriented, mismatched, or undersized panel leaving an opening around it.
Apply this label whenever such a visible opening is established, even if it is small, as long as it exposes space behind the filter plane or the frame rail/track behind the filters. Do not require the opening to be large or oversized.
Exclude only:
- The internal baffle channels within a single, intact, properly seated filter (these are the filter's normal slots, not a gap).
- Reflections and shadows. A bright highlight, a dark band, or a colored shape that is only a reflection on the filter surface is NOT a bypass gap—confirm the feature is an actual opening exposing the space behind the filter plane before applying the label.
- Grease staining, frame rails, and handles by themselves.
- An entirely empty filter slot, which is a missing filter rather than a bypass gap.
Darkness alone neither establishes nor negates a gap; judge clearly visible evidence. If an opening is visible at a filter edge or seam, apply the label even when the rest of the bank is in shadow.
In the classification explanation, identify the opening's location (which filters/edge) and the visible evidence distinguishing it from a filter's own baffle channel or a reflection.
